Madrasas and duksi in Kenya teach Quran recitation and memorisation to large numbers of children, but they are often administered informally, with attendance, memorisation progress, and fees recorded in exercise books or not recorded at all. Parents have limited access to reliable information about their children’s progress, and fee payments are not linked to invoices. Existing Quran applications primarily serve individual learners, while conventional school management systems lack Quran-specific functionalities. To address these challenges, this project developed Digital Madrasa, an integrated mobile application for managing madrasas in Kenya. The system was developed using the Agile methodology, with React Native (Expo) and TypeScript for the mobile application and Supabase, incorporating PostgreSQL, authentication, storage, and Edge Functions, for the backend. Each madrasa operates as a separate tenant, with its records protected by Row Level Security across all database tables. The application serves madrasa owners, teachers, parents, and students and provides student admission, class management, manual and QR-code attendance tracking, Quran memorisation progress monitoring, recitation recording with teacher review, parent-child linking approved by the madrasa, fee invoicing with M-Pesa payment, notifications, and multilingual support in English, Kiswahili, Somali, and Arabic. Unit, functional, and user interface testing demonstrated that the core features worked as required and that users could not access records outside their respective madrasa or authorised roles. All 74 unit tests and 56 functional test cases passed. However, M-Pesa, email, and SMS integrations currently operate through mock providers, and testing on physical mobile devices remains to be completed. The project demonstrates the feasibility of developing a secure, integrated madrasa management application tailored to the Kenyan context.

The Holy Quran is memorised and recited by Muslims as the word of Allah (SWT), and its memorisation (Hifz) together with the rules of correct recitation (tajweed) has been passed down through Quranic schools for centuries. Boyle (2004) describes these schools as institutions that both preserve a religious tradition and adapt to the societies around them. In Kenya, and particularly in the Coast, North Eastern and Nairobi regions, they are known as duksi or madrasa. They meet in mosques, homes and community buildings, admit children from about four years of age and teach recitation, memorisation and basic religious knowledge. Mwaura, Sylva and Malmberg (2008) evaluated the community Madrasa preschool programme in Kenya, Uganda and Zanzibar and found measurable cognitive benefits for participating children, showing that madrasa-based education can be structured and assessed.

The status of these institutions is changing. Ndzovu (2023) identifies the absence of a standardised syllabus and record-keeping as recurring concerns of the traditional madrassa system in Kenya, and in June 2026 the national government announced plans to integrate madrassa and duksi education into the national education system (Kihaki, 2026). Integration presupposes that a madrasa can produce reliable records of enrolment, attendance and learner progress, which most keep on paper or not at all.

The conditions for a mobile solution are present. The Communications Authority of Kenya (2023) reported 66.4 million mobile SIM subscriptions, a penetration rate of 131.3 per cent, and the Kenya National Digital Master Plan 2022–2032 makes the digitisation of services a national priority (Ministry of ICT and the Digital Economy, 2022). Consumer Quran applications already show that recitation practice can be supported on a phone, but they are built for individual learners and do not model the institution in which a teacher, a parent and a student share responsibility for a child's progress.

This project responds to that situation. Digital Madrasa is a mobile application that brings madrasa administration and Quran learning together in one secure platform, in which each madrasa keeps its own private records of admission, attendance, memorisation, recitation and fees, and shares them only with the teachers, parents and students entitled to see them.

Madrasas in Kenya lack standardised systems for recording admission, attendance, memorisation progress and fees. Records are usually kept in exercise books held by individual teachers; they are easily lost, cannot be summarised for the institution and cannot be shared with parents. Parents therefore have little reliable information about whether their child attends, how far the child has memorised, or what fees are owed. Recitation can only be assessed when a teacher hears each learner in turn, so in large classes feedback is infrequent, and fees are collected in cash or by M-Pesa with no link to an invoice or receipt.

Existing software addresses only parts of this problem. Quran applications support individual practice but have no teacher role, parental access, attendance register or fee records, while general school management systems have no Quran-specific functions such as memorisation tracking by juz or recitation review. Neither is designed for many independent madrasas, each of which must be able to trust that its records cannot be seen by another.

The problem this project addresses is therefore the absence of a secure, multi-tenant mobile application that unifies madrasa administration with Quran learning and gives owners, teachers, parents and students the information each of them needs.

text: 2.2 Challenges in Traditional Madrasa Administration and Quran Learning

runs: Traditional madrasa administration and Quran learning in Kenya face several challenges that affect the efficiency of institutional management and the monitoring of students' academic progress. Most madrasas are founded and run by communities, mosques or individual teachers and rely on manual administrative procedures (Boyle, 2004; Aden, 2017), which can make record keeping, attendance tracking, fee management and communication between teachers and parents difficult. Additionally, the absence of standardised syllabi and records limits the ability of teachers and administrators to maintain accurate and accessible student records (Ndzovu, 2023). These challenges highlight the need to examine existing administrative practices and identify areas where digital technologies could improve the management and delivery of madrasa education (Ministry of ICT and the Digital Economy, 2022).

text: 2.2.1 Informal Record Keeping and Lack of Standardisation

runs: Quranic schools are among the oldest continuously operating educational institutions in the Muslim world. Boyle (2004) describes their core pedagogy as the memorisation and correct recitation of the Quran under the close supervision of a teacher. In Kenya this tradition is carried by the duksi, which concentrate on recitation and memorisation, and by madrasas, which add Arabic, Fiqh and Islamic history. Most are founded and run by communities, mosques or individual teachers rather than by the state.

Aden (2017) notes that Islamic and secular education in Kenya have largely developed in parallel, with learners attending the madrasa before or after the public school day. Ndzovu (2023) highlights the absence of a standardised syllabus as a persistent issue, and the same lack of standardisation extends to records. An owner or head teacher admits learners, allocates them to classes and collects fees, while each teacher keeps his or her own notebook of attendance and of how far each learner has memorised. Such records are easily lost, give the institution no single view of a learner, and cannot identify a child who moves between classes or madrasas. With madrasas now to be integrated into the national education system (Kihaki, 2026), reliable records have become a necessity. The community Madrasa preschool programme, evaluated by Mwaura et al. (2008), shows that madrasalinked education can be organised and assessed when it is structured.

text: 2.2.2 Limited Parental Visibility and Assessment Workload

runs: Parents usually learn about attendance and progress informally, at pick-up or only when a problem has become serious. Fan and Chen (2001), in a meta-analysis, found a small to moderate but practically meaningful relationship between parental involvement and academic achievement, and Emerson et al. (2012) conclude that engagement is most effective when it is focused on the child's own learning. Epstein (2018) identifies regular school-to-home communication as one of the core types of family involvement. A madrasa that cannot tell parents how their child is doing loses this support.

Recitation must be heard to be assessed, so a teacher's capacity to give individual tajweed feedback is limited by class size and time; in the traditional method each learner recites in turn under the close supervision of the teacher (Boyle, 2004). In large classes learners may therefore recite to the teacher only occasionally, and persistent errors can go uncorrected between sessions.

Because madrasas are administered informally (Ndzovu, 2023), fees are typically recorded by hand and reminded verbally. Payments made in cash or by M-Pesa are not linked to an invoice, which makes balances hard to reconcile and disputes hard to resolve. Communication between the madrasa and families relies on phone calls and word of mouth, and parents who speak Kiswahili, Somali or Arabic rather than English may be excluded from written notices. At the same time Kenya is highly connected: the Communications Authority of Kenya (2023) reported a mobile penetration of 131.3 per cent, and the Kenya National Digital Master Plan 2022–2032 commits the government to the digitisation of services (Ministry of ICT and the Digital Economy, 2022). The phone that parents already use for MPesa is therefore a practical channel for records, payments and notices.

The Ministry of Education operates NEMIS, which links each learner to a unique identifier and reports national indicators for registered institutions (Ministry of Education, n.d.); a replacement, the Kenya Education Management Information System, was announced in 2025 (Tongola, 2025). NEMIS is described as a web-based data management solution that collects data from education institutions, processes and reports on designated indicators, and tracks the performance and mobility of learners and teaching staff (Ministry of Education, n.d.).
Strengths and limitations.

The strength of NEMIS is its national coverage: every learner in a registered institution has a unique identifier that follows the learner between schools. It serves national planning and reporting, however, rather than the day-to-day running of an institution. It does not record Quran memorisation or recitation, offers no parent view or fee management, and does not yet cover community madrasas and duksi, whose integration into the national education system has only recently been announced (Kihaki, 2026). runs: Al-Fraihat et al. The dedicated madrasa systems (QuranPortal, Origin E Madarsa, Alif Cloud and Sudoor HMS) do track memorisation, but they are designed for other markets: none documents M-Pesa payment, none offers a Kiswahili or Somali interface, and none documents students recording their recitation for later review by the teacher (Alif Cloud, n.d.-a; Origin Softwares, n.d.; QuranPortal, n.d.; Sudoor HMS, 2026). Alsharhan and Ramsay (2020) show that speaker gender, dialect and training size materially affect Arabic speech recognition. Automated tajweed feedback can therefore support, but not replace, the teacher. A static attendance QR code can be photographed and shared, so it proves presence only if it changes and is verified by the server.

text: 2.4 Concepts and Technologies Underpinning Integrated Education Systems

runs: Beyond individual products, the literature describes the architectural and technological concepts on which shared, multi-institution education platforms are built. This section reviews these concepts independently of any particular system.

Where many independent organisations share one application, the application is multi-tenant. Bezemer and Zaidman (2010) observe that multi-tenancy reduces operating cost but makes isolation between tenants a central engineering concern, and Alkhalil, Sahandi and John (2017) found that perceived security shapes the decision to move records into the cloud. Within each tenant, role-based access control assigns permissions to roles rather than to individuals (Sandhu et al., 2000), which suits institutions such as madrasas in which owners, teachers, parents and students need different access. Database-level mechanisms such as PostgreSQL Row Level Security allow the database itself to decide which rows each user may read or change (PostgreSQL Global Development Group, n.d.).

text: 2.4.2 Cross-Platform Mobile Development and Cloud Backends

runs: Cross-platform frameworks allow one codebase to serve several mobile platforms, at the cost of some access to platform-specific features (Biørn-Hansen et al., 2018). React Native is one such framework, in which applications written in JavaScript or TypeScript render native interface components (React Native, 2026). Managed backend platforms such as Supabase provide a hosted PostgreSQL database, authentication, file storage and server-side functions as services (Supabase, 2026), which reduces the infrastructure a small development team must operate.

Holmes, Bialik and Fadel (2019) argue that artificial intelligence in education should augment rather than replace the teacher. VanLehn (2011) found that intelligent tutoring approached the effectiveness of human tutoring, and Neri, Cucchiarini and Strik (2008) showed that automatic pronunciation feedback improved learners' speech. Kornell (2009) found that spacing study over time is more effective than cramming, which supports scheduled revision of memorised passages. Together with the limits of automated tajweed assessment noted in Section 2.3.8, these findings suggest that recitation technology should support the teacher's judgement rather than replace it.

Sommerville (2016) distinguishes development testing of components, release testing against requirements, and user testing. For applications shared by many institutions, the most important functional tests are those that prove a user cannot reach another institution's records or act outside their role, so refusals must be tested as well as successes. Usability can be measured with the System Usability Scale, a ten-item questionnaire that yields a score from 0 to 100 (Brooke, 1996) and suits users with limited experience of mobile applications, while field testing with real users on their own devices shows whether a system works outside the development environment (Sommerville, 2016).

This chapter reviewed madrasa education and administration in Kenya and the challenges of informal records, limited parental visibility, assessment workload and fee management. It then reviewed existing related systems: NEMIS serves national reporting, QuranPortal focuses on memorisation tracking, and Origin E Madarsa, Alif Cloud and Sudoor HMS offer fuller madrasa or hifz management, while general learning platforms, school administration software and Quran applications support teaching, administration or individual practice. None of the reviewed systems is designed for Kenyan madrasas: none documents M-Pesa payment, none offers a Kiswahili or Somali interface, and none documents recorded recitation review by the teacher. Finally, the chapter reviewed multi-tenancy, rolebased access control, cross-platform development and teacher-centred recitation technology. The next chapter describes the development methodology.

A development methodology defines how the work of building a system is organised: how requirements are gathered, how design and implementation proceed, and how the product is checked and delivered. This chapter explains why an Agile approach was chosen for Digital Madrasa and describes each phase of the development cycle as it was applied in the project.

Agile emphasises working software, collaboration and responding to change over following a fixed plan (Beck et al., 2001). It delivers a usable version of the software early and improves it in short cycles called sprints, each ending with a working increment that can be reviewed (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). Unlike the Waterfall model, in which each phase is completed before the next begins, Agile allows requirements to be refined as the system takes shape (Sommerville, 2016).

Agile suits this project because madrasa practices vary and many requirements, such as how parents should be linked to children or how fees should be targeted, became clear only when a working version could be tried. Each sprint delivered one complete capability, from the database rules to the screens, and was verified against the live backend before the next began. Figure 3.1 shows the cycle.

title: Agile development methodology used in the project

runs: The development of the Digital Madrasa application followed the Agile methodology, which supports iterative development, continuous evaluation, and improvement throughout the software development lifecycle. The process was organised into several phases, each addressing a specific aspect of system development, from identifying user requirements to designing, implementing, testing, and reviewing the application. This approach enabled the development process to remain organised while ensuring that the system's features aligned with the needs of madrasa owners, teachers, parents, and students. Feedback, testing results, and identified issues were used to guide improvements during development. The following subsections describe the key phases undertaken in developing the Digital Madrasa application, including requirements gathering, system design, implementation, testing, deployment, and review.

Requirements was identified from the literature on madrasa education and parental involvement, from a review of existing education management systems and Quran applications, and from the questionnaires and interviews with madrasa stakeholders (Appendix A.1). They were written as user stories, for example "As a parent, I want to see my child's attendance and fees so that I do not have to wait for pick-up", prioritised into a product backlog, and organised into two modules:
Administration module:
madrasa registration, student admission, classes, staff, attendance, fees and payments, announcements and messages.
Quran learning module:
memorisation progress, assignments, grades, recitation recording and review, and certificates.

The design phase translated the requirements into the models presented in Chapter Five: the class diagram, the entity relationship diagram and database schema, use case, sequence and activity diagrams, and wireframes of the main screens. The architecture was built around React Native with Expo for the mobile interface and Supabase for authentication, the PostgreSQL database, file storage and server functions. Security rules were designed into the database from the start, so that each madrasa's records are isolated by Row Level Security.

Development proceeded in sprints recorded in the project's Git history. The first sprint (23 August 2026) produced the multi-tenant database, authentication and the screens for all four roles. The second (16 September) added the server functions, automated backups and continuous integration. Later sprints connected the live backend and the recitation storage workflow (19 September), teacher recitation review and parent access to a child's recitations (22–23 September), QR attendance (23 September) and targeted invoicing (24 September). The final sprint (25–30 September) added written work and certificates, M-Pesa payments, push, e-mail and SMS notifications, and complete Kiswahili, Somali and Arabic translations.
Testing was carried out within every sprint to verify that new features worked and did not break existing ones. The testing types included:
Unit testing:
verifying individual functions such as input validation, QR token signing and MPesa callback handling.
Functional testing:
scripted calls to the deployed backend as each role, checking that permitted actions succeed and forbidden ones are refused.
User interface testing:
checking each screen on an Android emulator and in the web build at phone size.
Performance testing:
measuring response times of the main screens and database queries.

The database, storage and server functions were deployed to a hosted Supabase project from the first sprint, so every increment was tested against the real backend. The mobile application was run through Expo Go on an Android emulator, and build profiles were prepared to produce an installable Android package (APK) for distribution.

At the end of each sprint the working increment was reviewed against the requirements, and defects found in testing were fixed before new work began. Reviews led, for example, to the rotating QR code for attendance, to requiring the madrasa's approval before a parent can see a child, and to a faster form of the database access rules after performance testing.

This chapter explained the choice of an Agile methodology for Digital Madrasa and described its six phases as applied in the project: requirements, design, development, testing, deployment and review. The iterative approach allowed the system to adapt to the needs of four different roles while delivering a working, tested increment at the end of every sprint. The next chapter presents the requirements gathering and analysis in detail.

text: CHAPTER FOUR: REQUIREMENTS GATHERING AND ANALYSIS

runs: This chapter describes how the requirements for Digital Madrasa were gathered and analysed. It explains the data collection approach and methods, summarises the evidence gathered from madrasa owners and teachers, parents, students and secondary sources, and derives the functional and nonfunctional requirements and the stakeholders of the system. It closes with the challenges met during requirements gathering.

The process aimed to understand how madrasas currently record attendance, memorisation and fees, how parents follow their children's progress, and how recitation is assessed, and which technical and legal constraints the system must respect.

A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining qualitative and quantitative data so that the strengths of each compensate for the limitations of the other (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). Qualitative data came from in-depth interviews with madrasa owners and senior teachers, informal interviews with parents and students, and observation of how attendance is taken and recitation is assessed. Quantitative data came from structured questionnaires for each stakeholder group (Appendix A.1). Document analysis of published studies, government reports and the documentation of Supabase, Expo and Safaricom Daraja supplied the technical constraints (Supabase, 2026; Expo, 2026; Safaricom, 2026).
The qualitative data explained
why
madrasas work as they do, while the questionnaires indicated
how common
each practice and problem is. Together they ensured that the requirements reflected real madrasa practice rather than assumptions.

Both primary and secondary data collection methods were used. Primary data are collected directly from participants for the purpose of the study, while secondary data are existing data collected for other purposes (Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill, 2019). Primary data was collected directly from madrasa owners, teachers, parents and students. Secondary data came from published research, government reports and technical documentation. The main techniques were:
Questionnaires for madrasa owners and teachers, parents and students.
In-depth interviews with madrasa owners and senior teachers.
Informal interviews with parents and, with parental consent, students.
Observation of attendance taking and recitation assessment in madrasa sessions.
Review of relevant studies, government reports and similar systems.

Primary data collection focused on the people who run and use madrasas. Participants were selected by purposive sampling, which deliberately selects people who have direct experience of the subject being studied (Etikan, Musa & Alkassim, 2016). A total of 47 participants were involved in the study from madrasas in Kajiado and Nairobi counties. Table 4.1 shows the participants.

Interviews were semi-structured, which allows the researcher to cover a set of themes while following up on participants' answers (Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill, 2019), and focused on how participants record attendance, memorisation and fees, how parents are kept informed, how recitation is assessed, and what would make them trust a madrasa application. The questionnaires used closed questions so that responses could be summarised in charts.

Interview and observation notes were analysed thematically, by identifying, analysing and reporting patterns within the data (Braun & Clarke, 2006): statements were grouped into recurring themes, and each theme was mapped to a system requirement. Questionnaire responses were counted per option and presented as pie charts, each followed by an interpretation and the feature of the system that responds to it. Each stakeholder questionnaire contained ten questions.

Table 4.2 summarises the requirements expressed by madrasa owners and teachers, which were the primary input to the design. Tables 4.3 and 4.4 summarise the themes from interviews with parents and students.

runs: Madrasa Owner and Teacher Questionnaire Analysis

A total of twelve madrasa owners and teachers completed the questionnaire. Its purpose was to understand how attendance, memorisation progress and fees are currently managed, and how ready madrasas are to adopt a mobile application. The ten questions are reproduced in Appendix A.1, Section A.
Question 1: How is student attendance currently recorded in your madrasa?
Analysis:

Attendance records are weak or absent. Half of the respondents, 6 of the 12 (50.0%), use an exercise book or register, and 1 (8.3%) uses a wall chart. A further 3 (25.0%) rely on the teacher's memory alone and 2 (16.7%) do not record attendance at all, so in 5 of the 12 madrasas (41.7%) there is no written record of whether a child attended. No respondent chose "Other".
System solution:

The system provides a digital attendance register for each class and QR-code attendance, in which a student scans a code on the teacher's phone that changes every 30 seconds, so attendance is recorded once, cannot be forged and is summarised on the dashboard.
Question 2: How is a student's Quran memorisation progress recorded?
Analysis:

Memorisation progress is held mainly in teachers' heads. The most common answer was that the teacher remembers (5, 41.7%), followed by writing it in a book (4, 33.3%). Two respondents (16.7%) tell the parent verbally and 1 (8.3%) does not record progress. In total, 8 of the 12 (66.7%) keep no written record of how far each child has memorised.
System solution:
Teachers record memorisation surah by surah in the app. The system calculates the juz completed and the passages due for revision, and shows them to the student and the approved parent.
Question 3: How are fees recorded and communicated to parents?
Analysis:

Fee records are fragmented. Five respondents (41.7%) use a written receipt book, 3 (25.0%) rely on verbal reminders, 3 (25.0%) rely only on M-Pesa messages and 1 (8.3%) keeps no formal record. None of the methods links a payment to an invoice, which explains the balance disputes reported in the interviews.
System solution:

The owner defines fee structures and issues numbered invoices to the whole madrasa, a class or one student. Parents see each invoice and pay it by M-Pesa, and the system issues a receipt and updates the balance automatically.
Question 4: How many students are enrolled in your madrasa?
Analysis:

Most madrasas surveyed are small to medium institutions. Five respondents (41.7%) have 50–100 students, 3 (25.0%) have fewer than 50 and 3 (25.0%) have 101–200, while only 1 (8.3%) has more than 200. Even at 50–100 students, keeping attendance, memorisation and fee records by hand for every child is a considerable clerical load for one owner or teacher.
System solution:
Each madrasa is set up as its own workspace that scales from a handful of students to several hundred, with classes, rosters and records created inside the app rather than in separate exercise books.
Question 5: How do you communicate announcements to parents?
Analysis:

Announcements reach parents through informal channels. Four respondents (33.3%) pass messages through the children and 4 (33.3%) use WhatsApp groups, 3 (25.0%) make phone calls and only 1 (8.3%) uses printed notices. Messages sent through children or calls are easily lost and leave no record of who was informed.
System solution:
The owner or teacher posts an announcement once in the app, and it is delivered to the inbox of every parent concerned, with push, e-mail or SMS notification according to each parent's preferences.
Question 6: How often is each student's recitation individually assessed?
Analysis:

Individual assessment is limited. Only 2 respondents (16.7%) hear every student in every session; 4 (33.3%) do so several times a week, 4 (33.3%) once a week and 2 (16.7%) rarely. Half of the madrasas therefore assess each child individually once a week or less.
System solution:
Students record recitations between sessions, and the teacher reviews them in a queue, giving a score and comments without needing class time for every learner.
Question 7: How are new students admitted and identified?
Analysis:

Formal admission is uncommon. Five respondents (41.7%) keep no admission record at all and 3 (25.0%) record names without a number, so only 4 (33.3%) can identify each child uniquely. Without a unique number a child who changes class or madrasa cannot be traced.
System solution:
The owner admits each student in the app, and the system generates a unique admission number (DM-YYYY-NNNN) that parents later use to request a link to their child.
Question 8: Do you use a smartphone for madrasa work?
Analysis:

Smartphone use is widespread: 7 respondents (58.3%) already use a smartphone daily for madrasa work and 4 (33.3%) occasionally, so 11 of the 12 (91.7%) could run a mobile application on a device they own. Only 1 (8.3%) does not use one.
System solution:
Digital Madrasa is a mobile application that runs on the Android phones owners and teachers already carry, so no computer or extra equipment is required.
Question 9: Which language would you prefer for a madrasa application?
Analysis:

Language preferences are diverse. Kiswahili and Somali were each chosen by 4 respondents (33.3%), while English and Arabic were each chosen by 2 (16.7%). An English-only application would therefore suit only a sixth of the owners and teachers surveyed.
System solution:
The interface is available in English, Kiswahili, Somali and Arabic, and each user chooses their own language, with Arabic shown right to left.
Question 10: Would you use a mobile application to manage your madrasa?

title: Willingness to adopt a madrasa management application

runs: Analysis:

There is strong willingness to adopt: 9 of the 12 respondents (75.0%) would use a mobile application to manage their madrasa and 2 (16.7%) might, while only 1 (8.3%) would not. The respondent who declined cited unfamiliarity with apps.
System solution:
The system combines admission, attendance, memorisation, recitation review, fees and communication in one application with simple screens, large buttons and clear summaries to support adoption.
Parent Questionnaire Analysis
A total of twenty parents completed the questionnaire. It focused on how parents follow their children's madrasa education, pay fees and would use a mobile application (Appendix A.1, Section B).
Question 1: How do you currently learn about your child's attendance and progress?
Analysis:

Parents are informed informally or not at all. The largest group, 8 of the 20 (40.0%), learn about their child at pick-up, 5 (25.0%) through a phone call from the teacher and 3 (15.0%) at parents' meetings. Four parents (20.0%) said they are not informed. No parent receives a written or regular report.
System solution:

A parent links to a child using the admission number and date of birth; once the madrasa approves the link, the parent sees the child's attendance, memorisation, grades, recitations and fees, and receives notifications.
Question 2: Would you pay madrasa fees through M-Pesa in a mobile application?

title: Willingness to pay fees via M-Pesa

runs: Analysis:

There is strong demand for mobile payment: 15 of the 20 parents (75.0%) would pay fees through M-Pesa in an application and 4 (20.0%) might, while only 1 (5.0%) would not. In total, 19 of the 20 (95.0%) were open to the feature.
System solution:
The parent pays one or several invoices through an M-Pesa prompt on their phone. The amount is calculated by the server, and the receipt appears in the app as soon as payment is confirmed.
Question 3: How do you currently pay madrasa fees?
Analysis:

Payments are made informally. Nine parents (45.0%) pay cash to the teacher or owner, 8 (40.0%) send M-Pesa to a personal number and 3 (15.0%) send money through the child. None of these methods ties a payment to a specific invoice or month.
System solution:
Each fee is issued as a numbered invoice, and the parent pays it through an M-Pesa prompt in the app, so the payment is recorded against the right child and invoice automatically.
Question 4: Do you receive a receipt when you pay fees?
Analysis:

Receipts are rarely issued. Nine parents (45.0%) never receive a receipt and 7 (35.0%) only sometimes, so only 4 (20.0%) always have proof of payment. This explains the balance disputes reported by owners in the interviews.
System solution:
A receipt is issued automatically as soon as an M-Pesa payment is confirmed, and the parent can see every receipt and the remaining balance in the app.
Question 5: How often would you like to receive updates about your child?
Analysis:

Parents want regular information. Half of them, 10 of the 20 (50.0%), would like weekly updates, 5 (25.0%) daily and 4 (20.0%) monthly; only 1 (5.0%) wants to be contacted only when there is a problem.
System solution:
Attendance, memorisation and reviews are visible to the approved parent as soon as they are recorded, and each parent can choose which notifications to receive.
Question 6: Do you have a smartphone?
Analysis:
Smartphone access is high: 16 parents (80.0%) have their own smartphone and 3 (15.0%) share a family phone, so 19 of the 20 (95.0%) can use a mobile application. Only 1 (5.0%) has no smartphone.
System solution:
The parent interface runs on an ordinary Android phone, and important notices can also be sent by SMS for parents who do not open the app often.
Question 7: Which language do you prefer for notices from the madrasa?
Analysis:

Most parents prefer a language other than English. Somali was chosen by 8 parents (40.0%) and Kiswahili by 7 (35.0%), while 3 (15.0%) chose English and 2 (10.0%) Arabic. Written notices in English alone would not reach 85.0% of these parents in their preferred language.
System solution:
Parents choose Kiswahili, Somali, Arabic or English for the whole interface, including their inbox and notifications.
Question 8: Which information about your child is most important to you?
Analysis:

Memorisation progress matters most: 9 parents (45.0%) chose it, followed by attendance (5, 25.0%), the fee balance (3, 15.0%) and the teacher's comments on recitation (3, 15.0%). Each of these items was chosen by some parents, so a parent view must show all of them together.
System solution:
The parent dashboard shows each approved child's juz memorised, attendance rate, outstanding balance and reviewed recitations on one screen.
Question 9: How comfortable would you be with your child's records being kept in an app that only you and the madrasa can see?

title: Comfort with digital storage of children's records

runs: Analysis:

Most parents accept digital records if access is restricted: 8 (40.0%) would be very comfortable and 7 (35.0%) comfortable, a combined 75.0%. Three (15.0%) were neutral and 2 (10.0%) uncomfortable, mainly because they were unsure who else could see the records.
System solution:
Each madrasa's records are isolated in the database, and a parent can see a child only after the madrasa approves the link, in line with the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019.
Question 10: Would you use a mobile application to follow your child's madrasa education?

title: Willingness of parents to use the application

runs: Analysis:
Parents are keen to use such an application: 15 (75.0%) said yes and 4 (20.0%) maybe, while only 1 (5.0%), the parent without a smartphone, said no.
System solution:
Parents create an account, request a link to their child and, once approved, follow attendance, progress and fees and message the madrasa from the same app.
Student Questionnaire Analysis

A total of fifteen students completed the questionnaire, with the consent of their parents (Republic of Kenya, 2019). The purpose was to understand how recitation is practised, assessed and revised, and how students would use a mobile application (Appendix A.1, Section C).
Question 1: How does your teacher assess your recitation?
Analysis:

Individual assessment is not universal. Seven students (46.7%) recite to the teacher individually, 5 (33.3%) are heard only as part of a group and 3 (20.0%) said their recitation is rarely assessed. More than half of the students (53.3%) therefore receive little individual feedback on their recitation.
System solution:
Students record a recitation in the app. The recording is stored privately, the teacher listens and gives a score and comments, and the student and approved parent see the review.
Question 2: Would recording your recitation on a phone help you practise?

Students welcome recorded practice: 6 (40.0%) strongly agree and 5 (33.3%) agree that recording on a phone would help, a combined 73.3%. Two (13.3%) were neutral, and 1 (6.7%) disagreed and 1 (6.7%) strongly disagreed, mainly because they do not have regular access to a phone.
System solution:
The app lets students record as often as they need, shows the passages due for revision, and provides the Quran text for reading offline.
Question 3: How often do you recite to your teacher on your own?
Analysis:
Students confirm the owners' answers. Only 4 (26.7%) recite individually every session, 5 (33.3%) a few times a week, 4 (26.7%) once a week and 2 (13.3%) rarely.
System solution:
Recording a recitation in the app lets a student be heard by the teacher between sessions, however large the class.
Question 4: How do you know which passages to revise?

title: How students choose passages to revise

runs: Revision is guided mainly by the teacher (7, 46.7%), while 5 students (33.3%) decide for
themselves, 2 (13.3%) are reminded by their parents and 1 (6.7%) does not revise regularly. Students who plan their own revision have no record to tell them which passages they are forgetting.
System solution:
The student dashboard lists the passages due for revision today, calculated from the memorisation the teacher has recorded.
Question 5: How many juz have you memorised?
Analysis:

Respondents were at different stages: 4 (26.7%) had memorised less than one juz, 6 (40.0%) one to five, 3 (20.0%) six to fifteen and 2 (13.3%) more than fifteen. Progress tracking must therefore work for beginners as well as advanced huffaz.
System solution:
Memorisation is recorded surah by surah, so progress is shown accurately whether a student has memorised a few short surahs or most of the Quran.
Question 6: Do you have access to a smartphone at home?
Most students use a family member's phone: 9 (60.0%) use a parent's phone, 2 (13.3%) a
sibling's and 2 (13.3%) their own, so 13 of the 15 (86.7%) have some access. Two (13.3%) have none.
System solution:
A student signs in to their own account on any family phone, and records are tied to the account rather than to the device.
Question 7: How do you practise recitation at home?
Analysis:

Home practice is common but unchecked. Six students (40.0%) read aloud alone, 5 (33.3%) listen to recorded reciters and 3 (20.0%) practise with a family member; only 1 (6.7%) does not practise at home. In most cases nobody qualified hears the student until the next class.
System solution:
Students can record their home practice and submit it for the teacher's review, and the Quran text is available offline for reading.
Question 8: How soon after reciting do you get feedback from your teacher?
Analysis:
Feedback is often delayed: although 7 students (46.7%) receive it immediately in class, 4 (26.7%) wait until the next session, 2 (13.3%) several days and 2 (13.3%) rarely receive any.
System solution:
When the teacher reviews a recording, the score and comments appear in the student's app straight away and remain available to re-read.
Question 9: Would seeing your memorisation progress in an app motivate you?
Analysis:
Visible progress would motivate most students: 7 (46.7%) strongly agree and 5 (33.3%) agree, a combined 80.0%, while 2 (13.3%) were neutral and 1 (6.7%) disagreed.
System solution:
The student dashboard shows the juz memorised, a progress bar of ayahs memorised and certificates awarded by the teacher.
Question 10: Which language do you prefer for using the app?
Analysis:

Students are more comfortable with English than their parents: 5 (33.3%) prefer English, 4 (26.7%) Kiswahili, 4 (26.7%) Somali and 2 (13.3%) Arabic. Within one family, the student and the parent may therefore prefer different languages.
System solution:
Because the language is a setting of each user, a student can use the app in English while the parent uses Somali or Kiswahili.

Secondary data provided background that complemented the primary data. A review of academic literature, government reports and existing systems (Chapter Two) showed that madrasa records in Kenya are largely informal and unstandardised (Ndzovu, 2023), that the government plans to integrate madrasa education into the national system (Kihaki, 2026), and that parental involvement is associated with better achievement (Fan & Chen, 2001). It also showed that Kenya's mobile penetration makes a phone-based system practical (Communications Authority of Kenya, 2023), that existing madrasa systems do not support M-Pesa or Kiswahili and Somali (Alif Cloud, n.d.-a; Origin Softwares, n.d.), and that automated tajweed assessment is not yet reliable enough to replace the teacher (Al-Kharusi et al., 2025).

Technical documentation shaped the feasible scope. The Supabase free plan provides the database, authentication, storage and server functions without a billing account, which made it possible to build the whole backend at no cost (Supabase, 2026). Safaricom's Daraja documentation defined how an STK push payment is started and confirmed through a callback (Safaricom, 2026), and the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 required consent and care in handling children's records (Republic of Kenya, 2019). These findings reinforced the need for an integrated system that combines madrasa administration, Quran learning, parental access and fee management.

Based on the analysed data, the requirements were grouped into functional and non-functional requirements, and the stakeholders were identified. Functional requirements describe the services a system should provide, while non-functional requirements are constraints on those services, such as security, performance and usability (Sommerville, 2016); the non-functional requirements were framed using the quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010 (International Organization for Standardization, 2011).
Functional Requirements

rows: The system shall allow a madrasa owner to register a madrasa and allow users to sign up, sign in, sign out and reset a forgotten password by e-mail.
The system shall give owners, teachers, parents and students separate interfaces, determined by the role stored in the database.
The system shall allow the owner to admit students with automatically generated admission numbers (DM-YYYY-NNNN), create classes and add teachers.
The system shall allow teachers to take attendance manually or by a signed QR code that changes every 30 seconds, which students scan with their phones.
The system shall allow teachers to record memorisation surah by surah, and calculate the juz completed and the passages due for revision.
The system shall allow teachers to set and mark assignments, record grades and award certificates.
The system shall allow students to record a recitation, store it privately and let the teacher play it back, score it and comment on it.
The system shall allow a parent to request a link to a child by admission number and date of birth, and show the child's records only after the madrasa approves the link.
The system shall allow the owner to define fee structures and issue numbered invoices to the whole madrasa, a class or one student.
The system shall allow parents to pay one or more invoices by M-Pesa, with the amount calculated by the server, and issue a receipt when payment is confirmed.
The system shall send announcements, messages and notifications by in-app inbox, push, email and SMS according to each user's preferences.
The system shall provide role-based dashboards and an interface in English, Kiswahili, Somali and Arabic.

runs: Non-Functional Requirements

rows: Every table shall be protected by Row Level Security so that each madrasa's records are private and each user can perform only the actions of their role; secrets shall exist only on the server.
Children's records shall be handled under the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019; recitation audio shall be stored privately and played only through short-lived signed links.
Dashboards should load in under 3 seconds on a 3G/4G mobile connection; access rules shall be written so that they are evaluated once per query.
Payments shall be settled exactly once for the amount the server calculates; admission and invoice numbers shall be unique within a madrasa.
The interface shall be simple enough for users with limited experience of mobile applications, with large buttons, clear summaries and four languages.
Failure of an external service shall produce a clear message rather than a crash; the database shall be backed up every three days.
The code shall be strictly typed, the schema managed through numbered migrations, and automated checks run on every change.
Important actions, such as approvals, invoices and payments, shall be recorded in an audit log.

text: 4.8 Challenges in Requirements Gathering and Analysis

runs: Several challenges influenced the requirements gathering process.
Diverse stakeholder needs:

owners prioritise records and fees, teachers prioritise simple attendance and review, and parents want timely information. Features were prioritised by how many roles they serve and how directly they address the problem statement.
Limited stakeholder availability:
madrasa sessions run early in the morning, in the evening and at weekends, which limited the time available for interviews and observation.
Sensitivity of children's data:

information about minors requires consent and care under the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 (Republic of Kenya, 2019). Questions were framed neutrally, students took part only with parental consent, and the system was designed so that a parent sees a child only after the madrasa approves the link.
Technical constraints:
features such as a validated tajweed recognition model and live M-Pesa credentials were beyond the project's resources, so the system was designed to accept them later without redesign.
Variations in madrasa practice:
madrasas differ in class levels, fee structures and languages, so the system lets each madrasa define its own classes and fees and offers four languages.

This chapter described how the requirements of Digital Madrasa were gathered through questionnaires, interviews, observation and document review, and how they were analysed. The findings that 41.7% of madrasas keep no written attendance, 66.7% keep no written memorisation record, 20.0% of parents are not informed at all and 95.0% of parents are open to paying by M-Pesa shaped the functional requirements, while security, privacy and payment integrity shaped the nonfunctional requirements. The next chapter presents the system design.

System design translates the requirements of Chapter Four into a blueprint for implementation. This chapter presents the design of Digital Madrasa using Unified Modeling Language (UML) diagrams and related models. Structural diagrams (the class, object and component diagrams) describe the static organisation of the system, while behavioural diagrams (use case, sequence and activity diagrams) describe how it responds to users and events (Object Management Group, 2017). The chapter also presents the database schema, including the entity relationship diagram, and the wireframes of the main screens. Particular attention was given to role-based access and to keeping each madrasa's records separate from every other madrasa.

The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is a standard graphical language for visualising, specifying, constructing and documenting the artefacts of a software system (Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005). UML 2.5.1 divides its diagrams into structure diagrams and behaviour diagrams: structure diagrams show the static structure of the objects in a system, independent of time (Object Management Group, 2017). They provide a blueprint of how data and objects are organised and help developers understand how the parts of the system fit together (Sommerville, 2016). Three structural diagrams are presented: the class diagram, the object diagram and the component diagram.

A class diagram shows a set of classes, interfaces and collaborations and the relationships among them, and is the diagram most commonly used to model the static design view of a system (Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005). The class diagram in Figure 5.1 shows the main classes of the system, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them. A Madrasa has many students, teachers, classes, fee structures and announcements. A Student belongs to one madrasa and has attendance records, memorisation progress, recitations and invoices, and a Parent is connected to a Student through a ParentStudentLink that the madrasa approves. Each Recitation may receive TajweedFeedback, which the teacher reviews.

An object diagram shows a set of objects and their relationships at a point in time; it is a snapshot of instances of the classes in a class diagram and is useful for illustrating a structure with concrete examples (Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005; Fowler, 2004). runs: A component diagram shows the organisation of and dependencies among a set of components, where a component is a modular, replaceable part of a system that provides and requires interfaces (Object Management Group, 2017; Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005). Figure 5.3 shows the two subsystems of Digital Madrasa. In the mobile app, the owner, teacher, parent and student user interfaces depend on a shared localisation component and an API client. The API client uses four interfaces provided by the Supabase backend: authentication, the data API of the PostgreSQL database, storage for recitation audio and the Edge Functions. The Edge Functions in turn use the database and storage, and they are the only components that call the external Safaricom Daraja and messaging services, so no secret key is held in the app.

Behaviour diagrams show the dynamic behaviour of the objects in a system, including their interactions and changes of state over time (Object Management Group, 2017). They show the flow of activities, the order of operations and how each actor interacts with the system, and guide implementation decisions. Three behavioural diagrams are presented: the use case, sequence and activity diagrams.

A use case diagram shows a set of use cases and actors and their relationships, and is used to model the functional requirements of a system from the point of view of its users (Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005). The system has four main users: the madrasa owner, the teacher, the parent and the student, with a platform administrator who oversees the madrasas. The owner registers the madrasa, admits students, manages classes and staff, and defines fees and issues invoices; because an owner is also a teacher, the owner can do everything a teacher does. Teachers take attendance, display the rotating QR code, record grades and assignments, review recitations and decide parent link requests. Students scan the class QR code, record recitations and view their progress. Parents create an account, request a link to their child, view the child's progress and invoices and message the madrasa. Figure 5.4 shows these interactions.

A sequence diagram is an interaction diagram that emphasises the time ordering of the messages exchanged between objects (Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005). Figure 5.5 shows recitation submission and review. The student's app requests a private upload link, uploads the audio to storage and asks the server to evaluate it; the server stores the recitation and a provisional result. The teacher then opens the review queue, plays the recording through a short-lived link and saves a score, which the student and the approved parent can see.

title: Sequence diagram for recitation submission and review

runs: An activity diagram shows the flow from activity to activity within a process, including decisions and alternative paths, and is used to model workflows (Booch, Rumbaugh & Jacobson, 2005). The activity diagram in Figure 5.6 shows QR attendance. The teacher opens the class attendance screen and the system displays a signed code that changes every 30 seconds. A student scans the code, and the server checks the signature, the time window, the class and the student's role before recording the student as present; an expired or wrong code is refused.

A database schema is the description of a database, specified during design, that defines its tables, attributes, data types and constraints (Elmasri & Navathe, 2016). The schema of Digital Madrasa was designed from an entity relationship model. The entity relationship diagram, introduced by Chen (1976), represents entities, their attributes and the relationships between them; it is a data-modelling notation rather than one of the UML diagram types (Elmasri & Navathe, 2016), and it is therefore presented here as part of the database design rather than among the UML structural diagrams.

The entity relationship diagram in Figure 5.7 represents the core data of the system: the entities, their key attributes and the relationships between them, with cardinalities (1 and N). It was generated from the live database, so it matches the implemented schema. Every record carries the identifier of its madrasa, which is how the database keeps each madrasa's data separate.

Digital Madrasa uses a PostgreSQL database of 40 tables grouped into nine functional areas: tenancy and identity, access control, learning, attendance, recitation, finance, subscription, communication and operations, as shown in Figure 5.8. Every table that belongs to a madrasa carries its madrasa identifier, and Row Level Security is enabled and forced on all 40 tables, governed by 84 policies, so that users can read and change only the records their role allows (PostgreSQL Global Development Group, n.d.).

Figure 5.9 shows how the 40 tables are distributed across the functional areas. Communication is the largest area (8 tables, 20.0%), because announcements, messages, notification preferences and the outboxes for e-mail, SMS and push each need their own table. Tenancy and identity, learning and finance each account for 6 tables (15.0%), reflecting the three core concerns of the system: who belongs to which madrasa, what students learn, and what families owe and pay.

Several technical, practical and economic challenges arose during development. This section describes them and how each was addressed.
Multi-tenant security.

Supporting many madrasas and four roles in one system required every rule about who may see what to be written into the database as Row Level Security policies, and tested with accounts for every role.
Performance of access rules.

Performance testing showed that the original rule for reading a child's records became slower as the platform grew, so it was rewritten to be evaluated once per query and proven by a test to allow exactly the same records.
Handling money.
The app never sends an amount; the server derives it from the invoices, and a payment is settled on the server exactly once, even if the M-Pesa callback arrives more than once.
Device-only features.
Some features, such as push notifications, cannot be tested in Expo Go and need an installable build.

Some owners, teachers and parents have little experience with mobile applications and may prefer familiar paper registers. To encourage adoption the interfaces were kept simple, with large buttons and clear summaries, the application was translated into Kiswahili, Somali and Arabic, and payment uses M-Pesa, which families already use.

Limited resources affected the choice of tools. Free and open-source tools were used throughout: Expo, React Native, Visual Studio Code and the free tier of Supabase. M-Pesa, e-mail and SMS were developed against mock providers so that no paid accounts were needed; the same code switches to the real services when credentials are configured.

Long-term use requires ongoing maintenance. Database changes are made through numbered migrations, automated checks run on every change pushed to GitHub, and the database is backed up every three days. Keeping Expo, React Native and Supabase up to date and responding to feedback from madrasas will keep the system reliable.

This chapter described the implementation of Digital Madrasa with Visual Studio Code, React Native with Expo, and Supabase, presented the sign-up screen and the dashboards for owners, teachers, parents and students, and discussed the main development challenges: multi-tenant security, performance of access rules, payment integrity, user adoption, limited resources and continuous maintenance. The next chapter describes how the system was tested and deployed.

Testing establishes whether the system does what its requirements say, and deployment makes it available to its users. This chapter describes the testing of Digital Madrasa at three levels: unit tests of individual functions, functional and security tests of the deployed backend as each role, and user interface tests of the screens. It then summarises the results and describes the current and planned deployment.

Because the most important requirement is that no madrasa can see another's records and no user can act outside their role, tests checked that forbidden actions are refused as well as that permitted ones succeed.

Unit tests were written with Vitest for the logic that does not need a server: input validation, QR token signing, M-Pesa phone numbers and callbacks, notification rules, memorisation totals, invoice helpers, translation keys and the AI assistant's check on figures. This chapter presented the testing and deployment of Digital Madrasa. All 74 unit tests and 56 functional test cases passed, and 20 of the 27 interface checks were run and passed, with the remaining 7 awaiting a physical phone. The tests showed that the core features, including sign-in, admission, attendance, invoicing, M-Pesa payment and parent access, work as required, and that users cannot reach records outside their madrasa or role. The backend is deployed on Supabase, the app will first be shared as an APK, and future plans include the Google Play Store, live payment and messaging services, and a hosted web dashboard.

text: CHAPTER EIGHT: DISCUSSIONS, CONCLUSIONS, FUTURE WORKS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

runs: This chapter reflects on the outcomes of the project. It discusses how far each objective was achieved, outlines the work planned to take Digital Madrasa further, and makes recommendations for its continued development and use.
Objective 1: to analyse the challenges facing madrasas.

The literature review and the requirements gathering confirmed that madrasa records are informal and unstandardised, that parents have limited visibility, that assessing recitation places a heavy workload on teachers, and that fees are not linked to invoices. The questionnaires quantified these problems: 41.7% of the madrasas surveyed keep no written attendance record, 66.7% keep no written memorisation record, and 20.0% of parents receive no information about their child at all.
Objective 2: to review existing systems.

The review showed that Quran applications serve individual learners while education management systems have no Quran-specific functions, and that none keeps many independent madrasas separate or offers the languages of Kenyan madrasa communities. These gaps defined Digital Madrasa's design.
Objective 3: to design and develop the application.

This objective was achieved. The system was developed with React Native and Expo for the front end and Supabase for the backend. Owners, teachers, parents and students each have a dedicated dashboard, and admission, classes, manual and QR attendance, memorisation, assignments, recitation review, certificates, invoicing, M-Pesa payment and notifications were implemented against the live backend, with each madrasa's records isolated by the database and an interface in four languages.
Objective 4: to test the system.

Unit, functional and user interface testing confirmed that the core features work as required: all 74 unit tests and 56 functional test cases passed, and the tests showed that users cannot reach records outside their madrasa or role. This objective is partly ongoing: testing on physical phones and a usability study with real users remain to be done.

This project set out to address the challenges facing madrasas in Kenya, particularly in the Northeastern region (Mandera, Wajir and Garissa), where Quran learning institutions continue to rely largely on manual record-keeping, paper-based fee tracking and limited communication between teachers and parents. These practices make it difficult to monitor student progress, manage admissions and fees, and give parents a clear picture of their children’s learning. In response, the project developed
Digital Madrasa
, an integrated cross-platform application for managing madrasas in Kenya.

The system was built with React Native for the client application and Supabase for authentication, database management and backend services. Supabase was chosen over alternatives such as Firebase because it removed the need for a billing account, making the solution more affordable for institutions with limited resources. The application supports four user roles: student, teacher, parent and administrator. Each role has a dedicated interface suited to its responsibilities. A multi-tenant design keeps each madrasa’s data isolated, while features such as auto-generated admission numbers, parentto-child linking by admission number and M-Pesa fee payments address the day-to-day administrative needs of these institutions.

Beyond administration, the system supports the core purpose of a madrasa, which is learning the Quran. It provides a recitation feedback module aimed at helping students improve their tajweed, along with dashboards that let teachers track learner progress and let parents follow their children’s development remotely. This bridges the communication gap between the madrasa and the home, which was one of the key problems identified at the start of the project.

During development, several technical challenges were encountered and resolved. These included configuration errors in connecting to the Supabase backend, row-level security policies blocking user profile creation, and API rate-limit errors during authentication. They were overcome by using a database trigger to create profiles automatically and by refining the authentication flow. Resolving these issues strengthened both the reliability of the system and the researcher’s practical understanding of secure, cloud-based application development.

In conclusion, the project achieved its main aim of developing a digital solution that modernises how madrasas in Kenya manage students, teachers, parents and fees while supporting Quran learning. Digital Madrasa shows that affordable, locally relevant technology can improve the efficiency, transparency and accountability of Islamic educational institutions in underserved communities.

Although some features can be extended further, as outlined in the recommendations and future work sections, the system provides a solid foundation for the digital transformation of madrasa education in Kenya.
Building the Android package and publishing the app on the Google Play Store would make installation easier and more trusted, provide automatic updates and allow feedback to be collected from users.
The platform administrator's web console should be hosted and extended with reports, so that the madrasas on the platform, their subscriptions and their activity can be monitored from a browser.

text: 8.4.3 Integration of Push Notifications and Messaging

runs: Push, e-mail and SMS notifications are built but run on mock providers. Connecting the real providers and Safaricom's M-Pesa service, and confirming push delivery on physical phones, would give parents timely alerts about attendance, fees and reviews.

The system could remind students of passages due for revision using spaced repetition (Kornell, 2009), alert teachers to learners who fall behind, and replace the placeholder tajweed evaluator with a validated model trained, with consent, on recordings of Kenyan learners.

Many madrasas have unreliable internet access. Offline attendance and memorisation records that synchronise when a connection returns, in addition to the offline Quran text, would make the system usable in such areas.
Feedback should be collected regularly from owners, teachers, parents and students, beginning with a pilot in one madrasa, so that the system continues to meet real needs.

Because the system holds children's records, authorisation must remain in the database, every change to an access rule should be tested before deployment, and the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 must be followed. Multi-factor authentication should be offered, especially for owner and administrator accounts.
The application should be updated regularly to fix defects, keep Expo, React Native and Supabase current, and add features requested by users.

Collaboration with madrasa associations and the Ministry of Education would support adoption and help align the system's records with the planned integration of madrasa education into the national system (Kihaki, 2026; Tongola, 2025).
The application should be optimised for the low-cost smartphones common among families, by reducing their size and data usage and testing it on such devices.

Digital Madrasa achieved its objectives of analysing the problem, reviewing existing solutions, and building and testing a secure, integrated madrasa management application for Kenya. Its main contributions are the combination of madrasa administration with Quran learning, strict isolation of each madrasa's records, parent access approved by the madrasa, and fee invoicing linked to M-Pesa payment. The priorities for future work are publishing on the Google Play Store, live notifications and payments, smart revision alerts and better offline support.
